label: paraphrase
sentence: We cannot say what Origen taught, but Augustine taught that the punishment of the lost has no end.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Augustine wrote that after the final judgment there are two kingdoms, and that the lost suffer in degrees.

Augustine wrote: “After the resurrection, when the final judgment of all has been completed, there will be two kingdoms. Each will have its own clear boundaries. One is Christ’s, the other the devil’s. One is made up of the good, the other of the bad. Both are made up of angels and human beings. The first will have no will to sin, and the second no power to sin. Neither will have any power to choose death. The first will live truly and happily in eternal life. The second will drag out a wretched existence in eternal death, without the power of dying. For both the life and the death will be without end. Among the first there will be degrees of happiness, one happier than another. Among the second there will be degrees of misery, one more bearable than another.”

label: paraphrase
sentence: Many around Augustine found this hard to bear, and he called their moan in vain.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Augustine would not let them say the punishment ends.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Whether anyone condemned Origen for his teaching, our records do not say.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Gregory of Nyssa's teaching on the restoration of all things is not in our records, which rest on Cyprian and Augustine.

label: paraphrase
sentence: What we do hold is that Augustine answered many around him who found it hard to bear that the punishment of the lost has no end.

Augustine wrote: “So it is in vain that some, indeed very many, lament the eternal punishment and the endless, unbroken torments of the lost. They say they do not believe it will be so. They do not set themselves directly against Holy Scripture. But, prompted by their own feelings, they soften everything that seems hard. They give a milder sense to sayings they think were meant more to frighten than to be taken as literally true.”

label: paraphrase
sentence: Augustine said those people did not argue against Scripture, but softened down whatever seemed hard.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Augustine's words name no teacher whom those doubters followed.

sentence: Yes, we can read together, as among us a bishop preached to the people given to him.

label: paraphrase
sentence: The charge ran both ways, and the bishop's flock could stand before the bishop's seat and refuse to leave until the bishop heard them.

Augustine wrote: “‘Jesus answered and said to them, This is the work of God, that you believe in Him whom He has sent.’ This, then, is to eat the food: not the food that perishes, but the food that lasts to eternal life. Why do you get your teeth and stomach ready? Believe, and you have eaten already.”
Which words of your verse do you want to stay with first?

label: paraphrase
sentence: Among us, a name had to be set down before peace was asked for someone who had failed.

label: paraphrase
sentence: That name was then examined before the whole congregation, with its judgment.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Cyprian wanted each certificate to name the person.

Cyprian wrote: “For I hear that some certificates are given in a way that says, ‘Let so-and-so be received into communion along with his own people.’ The martyrs never did this in any case. Such a vague and blind request will soon heap blame on us. For it opens a wide door to say, ‘So-and-so with his own people.’ Then twenty or thirty or more may be brought to us. They may be said to be the relatives, in-laws, freedmen and household of the man who received the certificate. For this reason I beg you to name in the certificate those whom you yourselves see and have known. Name those whose repentance you see is very near to full satisfaction. Then send us letters that agree with faith and discipline.”
Do you want us to go further into how we dealt with those who failed, or into the saying itself?

label: paraphrase
sentence: Among us, communion is a formal standing within the one body, which a person can lose and be given back.

label: paraphrase
sentence: At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of communion for thinking differently.

label: paraphrase
sentence: A century and a half later, Augustine argued at book length that the ruling of that council was wrong.

label: paraphrase
sentence: Augustine never put Cyprian outside our communion.

Augustine wrote: “The Winnower will come and divide the bad from the good. Then there will be a bodily separation too. A separation in spirit comes before it now. In heart, always keep apart from the bad. In body, stay joined with them for a time, but with caution. Yet do not neglect to correct your own people, those who in any way are in your care. Do it by warning, by teaching, by urging, or by threats.”
Is it the rite of the table you are asking about, or the standing we call communion?
